newsitem.title: USA: U.S. appeals court sets aside FCC phone rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. appeals court sets aside FCC phone rules.

text.p: A federal appeals court Friday set aside key parts of landmark federal rules designed to pry open to competition the $100 billion local telephone market controlled by the regional Baby Bell phone companies.

The St. Louis-based court said the Federal Communications Commission lacked the authority to set reference prices for local calls as part of the agency's efforts to open the local market to long-distance companies and others wanting to offer local service.

The FCC rules spell out how new competitors can hook up to local phone networks, as well as the price the new entrants should pay for using the networks. The rules -- adopted last August but suspended by the court in the fall -- are meant to implement the communications law passed last year.
But the court, in a lengthy ruling, said the act "directly and straightforwardly assigns to the states" -- and not the FCC -- the authority to set prices for local phone service.
The FCC had ordered the Baby Bells and other local carriers to offer steep discounts to new competitors wanting to hook up to the Bell networks and offer their own local service.

Baby Bell officials claimed victory, saying their arguments won out over those of the FCC and long-distance carriers who had asked the court to back the agency's rules. "It's better than expected," said a spokesman for BellSouth Corp. "It's clear the court read the act and knows the intent of Congress."
